problem: The Latin word 'Resurgam' ends the chapter and carries its meaning, but most modern readers and listeners will not know it. A short in-line gloss keeps the effect.
new_text: Her grave is in Brocklebridge churchyard. For fifteen years after her death, it was marked only by a grassy mound. But now a gray marble tablet stands there, inscribed with her name and the single word: Resurgam—"I shall rise again."

problem: 'I need only call on memory where her answers will hold some interest': 'her' has no clear antecedent (memory is personified without warning). A listener will look for a woman.
new_text: Until now I have recorded the events of my insignificant life in detail: to the first ten years of my life I have given almost as many chapters. But this is not meant to be a full autobiography. I need only call on memory where its answers will hold some interest. So I now skip over a space of eight years almost in silence. A few lines will suffice to keep the thread connected.

problem: Jane asks 'And you don't live at Gateshead?' and Bessie answers 'I live at the lodge', which does not say whether that is yes or no. Saying the lodge is at Gateshead makes the answer clear.
new_text: "I live at the lodge there. The old porter has left."

problem: The pupil is called 'Adela' (11.40, 11.60 by Mrs. Fairfax; 11.65 by the narrator) and 'Adèle' (11.72 onward by the narrator). Mrs. Fairfax's English form can pass as her way of speaking, but in the narrator's voice at 11.65 it makes it look like two different names, especially when read aloud. Use 'Adèle' in the narration. Optionally, make Mrs. Fairfax's lines match or note that she uses the English form.
new_text: Fortunately, I had been taught French by a Frenchwoman. I had always made a point of speaking French with Madame Pierrot as often as possible, and had spent the last seven years memorizing a portion of French daily, working hard on my accent and imitating my teacher's pronunciation as closely as I could. I had developed a reasonable fluency and accuracy in the language and was unlikely to struggle much with Mademoiselle Adèle. She came and shook hands when she heard I was her governess. As I led her in to breakfast, I spoke to her in French. She answered briefly at first, but after we were seated at the table and she had studied me for about ten minutes with her large hazel eyes, she suddenly began chattering away.

problem: The whole paragraph is essentially one sentence: 'when I add that, now and then, when..., or when, while..., I climbed...—that then I longed... That then I craved...'. With nested 'when' clauses and a delayed main verb, a listener loses the thread. Splitting it keeps the wording and voice.
new_text: Anyone who wants to can blame me when I add this. Now and then I walked alone in the grounds, or went down to the gates and looked along the road; or, while Adèle played with her nurse and Mrs. Fairfax made preserves in the storeroom, I climbed the three staircases, pushed open the attic trapdoor, and stood on the roof looking out over the secluded fields, the hills, and the dim horizon. At such times I longed for a power of vision that could reach beyond that boundary, that could see the busy world, the towns, the regions full of life I had heard of but never witnessed. At such times I craved more practical experience than I possessed, more contact with my fellow human beings, more acquaintance with the variety of human character than was within my reach here. I valued what was good in Mrs. Fairfax and in Adèle, but I believed in the existence of other, more vivid kinds of goodness, and I wanted to see what I believed in.

problem: 'Mrs. Fairfax had requested a holiday for Adèle because she had a cold': 'she' could mean Mrs. Fairfax or Adèle.
new_text: October, November, and December passed. One afternoon in January, Mrs. Fairfax had requested a holiday for Adèle, who had a cold. Since Adèle backed the request with an enthusiasm that reminded me how precious holidays had been in my own childhood, I agreed, thinking it right to be flexible. It was a fine, calm day, though very cold. I was tired of sitting still in the library all morning. Mrs. Fairfax had just written a letter that needed posting, so I put on my bonnet and cloak and volunteered to carry it to Hay—a pleasant two-mile walk on a winter afternoon. After settling Adèle comfortably in her little chair by Mrs. Fairfax's fire, giving her the best wax doll (which I usually kept wrapped in silver paper in a drawer) and a storybook for variety, and answering her "Revenez bientôt, ma bonne amie, ma chère Mademoiselle Jeannette" with a kiss, I set out.
